conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. I’ll be using a short tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—you might hear it called the EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions that help us see whether you might be experiencing the baby blues, postpartum depression, or anxiety, all of which are very common and very treatable.

Everything you share stays confidential between you and our care team; the goal is to make sure you feel safe, heard, and supported. We’ll go through the questions one by one, focusing on how you’ve felt over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

I’ve noticed it’s definitely slipped away compared to before. I can still enjoy a few things—like when my baby smiles at me or when I manage to get outside for a short walk—but even those moments feel kind of muted, like I’m going through the motions more than really feeling happy.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often…maybe once or twice I cracked a small smile, but mostly I feel too tired and on-edge to find much funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Hardly at all. I’ll make little plans—like taking the baby to the park or meeting a friend for coffee—but when the time comes, it feels like another chore rather than something I’m excited about.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes, quite a lot of the time. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it must be something I’m doing wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed his sleepy cues. Even little things, like spilling a bottle or being late to an appointment, turn into “I’m a terrible mom” in my head.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, most of the time. My mind keeps jumping to awful “what-ifs”—like the baby stopping breathing in his sleep or me dropping him. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just race and I can’t settle them, even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, I have. Sometimes my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get enough air, even when nothing’s actually happening. It hits suddenly—like when I’m just folding laundry or walking to the mailbox—and I’ll think, “What if I can’t keep him safe?” or “What if I mess everything up?” It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and on edge.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, most of the time. It feels like the second I finish one task—feeding, changing, pumping—two more pop up. I can’t seem to get ahead, and I keep thinking, “If I can’t handle this, how will I ever manage anything harder?”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes, that’s been happening. I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off—rerunning every little thing I did wrong that day, worrying about the baby, worrying I’ll never feel like myself again. It takes me over an hour to drift off, and then I wake up a couple of times with my heart pounding before morning.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yes, most of the time. It’s like a gray cloud that just hangs there—even when the baby’s calm and things look “fine” on the outside, I still feel heavy and sad inside.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, sometimes. It’s not every day, but maybe once or twice this week I’ve just broken down—usually when I’m alone after the baby finally naps and the house is quiet. I’ll start thinking I’m failing him, and the tears just come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yes, it’s crossed my mind once or twice this week. It’s more like a fleeting “what if I just wasn’t here” when everything feels too much, but I haven’t made any plans and I don’t want to leave my baby—I just want the pain and pressure to stop.

Hearing how exhausted, anxious, and sad you've felt since your baby arrived touches my heart; it sounds as though the joy you expected has been replaced by a constant gray cloud of worry, guilt, and tears. You shared that even simple tasks feel overwhelming, that panic jolts you awake, and that fleeting thoughts of escape have surfaced-yet you clearly love your baby and want relief, not an end.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, minimal smiling and attributes inability to laugh to fatigue and tension, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Hardly at all" and describes anticipatory anhedonia—plans feel like chores, not enjoyable</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "quite a lot of the time" and gives multiple daily examples, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>The patient reports experiencing intrusive, racing anxious thoughts "most of the time" and being unable to settle them, which clearly aligns with the "Yes, very often" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, sudden panic-like episodes with racing heart, breathlessness, and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes severe, nightly sleep disturbance linked to unhappiness—takes >1h to fall asleep, wakes multiple times with anxiety—matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient affirms sadness "most of the time" and adds persistent, pervasive low mood despite external calm</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score ≥14 on the EPDS indicates probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>; your score of 24 far exceeds this threshold. You endorse core depressive symptoms (low mood, markedly reduced enjoyment, frequent crying, self-blame, impaired sleep) and prominent anxiety symptoms (near-constant worry, sudden palpitations, breathlessness). Item 10 indicates passive suicidal ideation, mandating immediate safety assessment. Taken together, these findings meet screening criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or local <med>perinatal mental health service</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Bring a trusted adult to the appointment for support and to help remember recommendations
3. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or your local emergency services if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
4. Begin evidence-based treatments recommended by your provider-options include <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, sertraline or other compatible <med>antidepressants</med> while breastfeeding
5. Plan small, manageable daily goals: 15-minute stroller walk, one balanced meal, one shower; celebrate completing each
6. Accept help with overnight feeds or household tasks so you can obtain 3-4 hour blocks of rest; good sleep reduces symptom severity
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress and adjust treatment
8. Continue attending <med>postpartum support group</med> or peer calls to reduce isolation and normalize recovery
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) interview

Symptoms endorsed  
- Marked anhedonia (minimal laughter/pleasure)  
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” frequent crying  
- Excessive guilt/blames self for routine infant-care issues  
- Near-daily, intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety; panic attacks  
- Sleep-onset and mid-night waking linked to ruminative worry  
- Sense of being overwhelmed, “can’t get ahead”  
- Passive self-harm ideation (no plan/intent)

Pattern  
Responses cluster in depressive (items 1,2,7,8,9) and anxiety (4,5) ranges; prominent guilt, anhedonia, and functional impairment. Passive suicidal thoughts present within past week.

Risk indicators  
- Suicidality: endorsed fleeting “what if I wasn’t here” → safety flag raised  
- Moderate–high depressive symptom load; anxiety symptoms equally prominent  
- Impaired sleep and coping; no reported support details

Screening impression  
Findings exceed perinatal mood/anxiety screening threshold; immediate safety assessment and referral for comprehensive perinatal mental health evaluation indicated.
